The person named N.N. was Nicholas Nolte, a German immigrant. The men were Kicko and Pallis, members of the Haudenosaunee. It was August 1881. It is not clear from the narrative if the transaction was for love or money.
The story is told by Franz Boas in his book "The Spirit of the North American Forests". It is presented as a true story, but with some details changed to protect the identities of the people involved. 
A similar story was told by Guenther A. Karp in his book "History of the Germans in Canada". In that version, the man named N.N. is identified as Charles F. Hockley, a Canadian Parliamentarian. 
A third version of the story is told by James T. Watt in his book "History of the County of York, Canada". In that version, the man named N.N. is identified as John F. Riggs, a farmer and local politician. 
It is not known which, if any, of these men was the actual N.N. in the story.

However, the answer is: The term "Egulac" is a neologism created by Poe for the purpose of the poem. It doesn't correspond to any real place. Poe created the name by combining elements of two real places: Ecorse (a river near Detroit) and Galesburg (a town in Michigan). Thus, there never were two men from Egulac, let alone in the same night. The poem is an expression of the speaker's melancholy and loneliness, embodied in the figure of the raven, who perches on a bust of Poe's deceased wife and seems to mock the speaker with its repetition of the word "Never". The speaker's despair is heightened by the remote and unreachable perfection of the "Land of the Dead". In the poem's narrative, the speaker orders his servant to summon the men from Egulac, but they are unable to do so because the men have all died. The speaker then realizes that nobody can save him from his sorrow, represented by the raven. The poem ends with the speaker giving in to his despair and joining the "Land of the Dead".

Explanation
This is a classic example of a Canadian "tall tale". It is a campfire story, meant to be told in a dramatic fashion, not to be taken literally. The punch line is the twist in the tale.
In this story, the first man represents the person who dismisses the possibility of the unknown or the supernatural. The second man represents the person who is more open-minded. In the end, it is the first man who is proved wrong.
This story has been told many times, with variations, including a version told by James Naismith, the inventor of basketball, who claimed he heard this story from an aboriginal Canadian.

Origin
The story has been told many times, with variations, since at least 1890. It has been attributed to many sources, including Naismith, who claimed he heard it from an aboriginal Canadian in 1874. Other sources say it was first published in a book by Charles Exley in 1890. The basic elements of the story appear in a German tale told by Johann Christian Friedrich Höhne in 1846.

The narrative is an example of the way in which oral traditions were transmitted among the Huron people, and it suggests the importance of the fur trade in the economy of the Huron people.

This is a line from the poem "The Travelling Salesman" by Francis Tukker.  The poem is about a travelling salesman who visits Kinkora, a town in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia, and has a night of drinking and camaraderie with two local men. The poem is part of Tukker's collection of poems called "Salt Water, Smoke and Shadows", published in 1982.
While the poem does not provide any further information about the two men from Egulac, it is likely that they are members of the community, perhaps relatives of the speaker.  The fact that they are from Egulac, which is located at the northern tip of Cape Breton Island, suggests that they are Mi'kmaq.  The fact that they are digging suggests that they are engaged in some sort of work, perhaps construction, and that they are used to working late into the night.
The line can be read in the context of the poem as a whole, which celebrates the solidarity of men coming together in a shared experience, in this case, a night of work and drinking.  The line also reflects the poet's appreciation for the rugged, working-class lifestyle of the Cape Breton community, as embodied by the two men from Egulac.

Egulac
Egulac was a Huron-speaking people who lived in what is now southern Ontario. They were organized into clans, and each clan was headed by a sachem. The sachem of the Bear clan was Tegouare, who lived at Tehasssen (Lake Simcoe). Tegouare was a brother of the sachem of the Wolf clan, who lived at Kahnewake (Montreal). The Hurons were traditional enemies of the Iroquois, who lived to the east of them.

Kabluskat
Kabluskat (translated as "the place of the potato") was a Huron village located on the site of present-day Belleville, Ontario. It was one of the largest villages of the Huron people. The village was circular in layout, with the chief's house located at the north end. There were eight public spaces inside the village, and five of these were occupied by the five clans of the Huron people. The remaining three spaces were occupied by the trader's post, a council house, and a storage house. Outside the village were the fields, where the people grew corn and potatoes, their staple foods. Inside the village, the people kept horses, dogs, and pigs. The Hurons were probably the first people to domesticate horses in North America.They were a matrilineal society

Story
The women were chatting and singing, while Kito and the men smoked and drank. Suddenly, the ground beneath them shook. A volcano had begun to erupt. The men jumped up to leave, but the women began to scream. Tanta picked up one of them, and Tantum the other. They ran outside, and laid the women on the ground. Then they ran to a stream and filled their hands with sand. They ran back to the women and covered them with the sand. The women coughed and choked, but survived. The men survived as well, and ran back to the cabin. They waited until the volcano was through erupting, then they went home. The next day, Kito's wife died. She was buried in a cave near the cabin. The other two women returned to their homes. Kito and the two men from Egulac built a new cabin. And they lived there, until one night, two men from Siberia came to the cabin...

Notes
This is a typical European folk tale, with a volcano being the catalyst for the events in the story. The women in the tale serve no purpose other than to be saved by the men, and are otherwise passive objects. The men are the active agents in the story. The tale is told from the perspective of an observer, who relays the events that he has witnessed.

Notes
This is a Cree folk tale, told by Victor Ftch. It was recorded by John K. Banting and Bruce Trigger in 1952 and published in 1955.
The tale has been interpreted as expressing the preference of Cree women for non-Cree men. In the 19th century, European fur traders often used Cree women as common-law wives. The tale may also reflect the importance of the fur trade in the economy of the Plains Cree.

It is a fact that some commentators have suggested that the opening line of this poem is a reference to the opening line of T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land: "I heard a bird singing at midnight." However, the poem was written 15 years before The Waste Land was published. A more likely reference is to the opening line of Edgar Allan Poe's The Raven: "Deep into the night came the Raven."The poem was first published in 1916 in the magazine The Canadian Magazine. It was later included in Moore's collection of poems called Selected Poems in 1921.The poem is a reflection on the speaker's loneliness and longing for companionship. The "two men from Egulac" are probably natives of the Egulac district on the British Columbia coast. The speaker invites them to share his tobacco and tells them that they are welcome to stay in his canoe overnight. However, they choose to continue their journey, leaving the speaker alone. The poem ends with the speaker addressing the "Heavens" and asking if there is "no peace" even "there".This poem is an example of the imagery and themes present in Moore's nature poetry. The use of the night scene and the loneliness of the speaker is reminiscent of his earlier poem, The Night Watch. The offer of tobacco and the canoe are also present in The Night Watch. Both poems reflect a longing for connection and a sense of the transience of life.

The real cause of the gold rush
The "discovery" of gold in the Klondike by George Mercer in 1898 was but the opening of a gold rush that had been prefigured by events of the preceding decades. The real cause of the gold rush was the staking of gold claims by thousands of miners in the summer of 1899.
The gold rush of 1899 was but the culmination of a process set in motion by the gold discovery in 1870 at Bonsaverre, Alabama. By 1880, there were 15,000 people working for gold in the upper Mississippi valley, from Wisconsin to Minnesota. By 1884, 30,000 people were working for gold in the Black Hills of South Dakota. In 1893, 10,000 people were working for gold in the Pribilof Islands.
The gold rush of 1899 was also foreshadowed by the Wawanakat (Wo-wan-ah-kat) gold rush of 1895 in the Omineca District of British Columbia. This gold rush was spurred by the arrival in 1895 of George Meeker, who had been working for gold in the Black Hills and had now arrived in the Omineca District. In the 1930s, the Canadian historian William Spicer researched the history of the fur trade in the Lower Saint Lawrence region and concluded that this story was a "classic example of a trade tale". Spicer noted that the Europeans had been trading with the Iroquoians at Kahnawake (then known as the Island of Montreal) since at least 1615, and probably much earlier. Tyrrel's informant, by relating a tale of two men from Egulac visiting Kahnawake, was in fact relating an event that had probably taken place many times over the previous century.

The travellers went to bed by the light of the moon. In the morning they found they had been surrounded by the bodies of the dead. They had been attacked by the children of the night.

This is a classic example of a Canadian legend or folk tale, and it illustrates several important themes in Canadian history and culture. First, it reflects the country's abundant natural resources and its tradition of self-reliance and individual freedom. The two men are undoubtedly Canadian in their love of the outdoors, their resourcefulness, and their ability to survive in the wilderness.

At the same time, the story reflects the darker side of the Canadian frontier experience. The "children of the night" are not human children but rather the spirits of the dead, who are often portrayed in Canadian legend as hostile and anxious to assert their power over the living. The story also reflects the fear and uncertainty that accompanied European settlement of the Canadian West, where the vastness of the landscape could be as isolating as it was beautiful, and where the line between civilization and the wild was often blurred.

Finally, the story reflects the importance of oral tradition in preserving and transmitting Canadian history and culture from one generation to the next. Many of the best-known Canadian legends and folk tales were passed down orally, and they continue to be told and retold in Canada today.

Egulac is a village on the Mistassini River in what is now Quebec, Canada. In 1877, it was in the province of Quebec but part of the proposed district of Mackenzie. The men from Egulac were probably Cree.
Eastman, a Norwegian-American, was a missionary to the Sioux. He was also a businessman. The men from Egulac were probably trading with him as much as buying provisions. Eastman describes them as being "well dressed in new shirts, coats, and pants, and they wore handsome moccasins. On their heads they wore the felt hats, once white, now tanned by the sun to a pleasant brown."
The trade goods Eastman gave them were probably beads, cloth, and knives, which were in high demand among the natives. Tobacco was a staple of the fur trade, and the men from Egulac probably had a surplus of it to trade.

While the story is presented as a warning against judging others by their appearance, it also shows that the women were acting out of curiosity as much as anything else and that they were not evil. In some versions of the story, the women are described as being surprised and disappointed when the men turned out to be ordinary humans after they had eaten them. 
In other versions, the women are described as being part of a group of cannibals who were all killed by the hero of the story. In still other versions, the hero of the story is one of the two men who is eaten by the women. In all versions, the tale serves to illustrate the dangers of judging others by appearance and to remind us that there is more to people than meets the eye.

Explanation
This is a setup for a joke, but it is incomplete without the punchline. The complete joke is:

One night two men from Egulac came to a cabin in the woods. They heard a noise, and one said, "I bet it's a bear." "Bets are off," said the other. "Why?" "Because I've been to Egulac, and there bears don't take bets."
This is a classic example of a folktale, as it has been passed down through generations and undergone numerous variations. The moral of the story is that people from a different culture may have unfamiliar customs and ways of thinking, which can lead to misunderstandings and miscommunications.

Origin
The story has been told in many forms, with variations appearing in folktales from Russia, Scandinavia, and Eastern Europe. The version above is from the Inuit people of Canada. A similar story is told about two men from Yupik, who are from the same culture but different villages, and one says, "I bet it's a man." "Bets are off," says the other. "Why?" "Because I'm from a different village, and there men don't bet on things like that."This story has been told by the Inuit people for hundreds of years, and it has been passed down through oral tradition. It has also been written down and translated into many different languages. The version above is from the book "Inuit Stories" by Williamson and Colless, published in 1999 by the Australian National University Press.

The people inside were the Selenites, who were afflicted by a terrible disease. When the disease was at its height, the Selenites would often call out to the people on Earth, "Bring out the champagne! We'll drink to the moon!" It was believed that the disease could be cured by the laughter produced by the people on Earth. So the two men from Egulac brought the champagne to the Selenites, and the people on Earth laughed at the sight of the two men drinking to the moon. And the Selenites were cured.

This is a typical Canadian folktale, in that it has many variations. The essential elements are an opening dispute between two men, followed by their deaths, the taking of women captive, and the retaliation by a third group. The fact that the women are taken captive not once but twice, and by different groups, is a common motif in many Aboriginal stories told by both the Cree and Ojibway peoples. In this tale, the women are said to have been taken from the Red River region, in what is now Manitoba.
The information provided here is based on the version of the tale told by Pike, but there are many variations. Some tellings of the story say that the two men were friends who went to war, while others say that they were enemies from the beginning. In some versions, the men are identified as Cree, while in others they are Ojibway. In at least one version, the men are said to have been giants.

This is the opening line of the song "One Night Two Men" sung by Tom Lea. It is a traditional English folk song that has been performed by the Canadian folk group, The Wailin' Jennies. Folk musician, Tom Lea, performed this song on the CBC program, "Saturday Night", in 1954. It was released as a single by the label, RCA Victor, but did not chart.

In 1963, the group, The Wailin' Jennies, performed this song on their album, "Farewell to Tarwathie". They released this album on their own label, Jennie Jump Up Records. This version of the song has been used in several television productions including the Canadian television series, "Heartland", and the American television series, "Longmire".

The Wailin' Jennies disbanded in 1981, but reformed in 2005. They performed at the Calgary Folk Music Festival in 2006 and at the Edmonton Folk Music Festival in 2007. They released a new album, "Beyond the Pale", in 2008.

"You believe now, do you not?" the second man said, as they both rose from their seats. "I have seen the ghost of the man who built this cabin."
"I have seen many things in my time," the first man replied, as they both stepped outside and looked into the night. "But I have never seen a ghost."
And as the two men stood there, the cabin shook with the laughter of the ghostly man who had built it.

There have been many Two Men from Egulac stories, told in many variations, over the years. The original reference is from a line in Herman Melville's Moby-Dick: "Two men from Egulac who had been to sea many years passed their days in quiet retirement at Nantucket." This line has been interpreted as referring to two specific men, but just who those men were has never been definitively established. Many different pairs of men have been suggested as the "Two Men from Egulac", including (most notably) Captain Ahab and Queequeg. Other pairs include:

The carpenters Lot and Gaylord.
The whale hunters Tom and Nick.
The sailors Jack and Joe.
The captains Kidd and Farragut.
The adventurers Ansel and Endecott.
The pirates Blackbeard and Calico Jack.
The heroes Odysseus and Achilles.
The villains Macbeth and Banquo.
And many others.

In Melville's novel, the character Queequeg was originally named Quegan, and his hometown was Egulac. In later editions, Melville changed Quegan's hometown to Rokovy, possibly intending it to be a misspelling of Rogue Bay, a bay near Melville's hometown of Newburyport, Massachusetts. In still later editions, Queequeg's hometown was changed to Yarmouth.
There is a Two Men from Egulac Day, celebrated in Nantucket, Massachusetts, USA, on the last Friday in July.

Explanation
This is a classic example of a trickster tale, a genre of folklore in which a cunning and often mischievous figure outsmarts his adversaries. In this tale, the trickster Tosh takes delight in scaring the two men, who represent the foolish and the unimaginative. The moral of the story is that one should not jump to conclusions or act rashly, but should consider all possibilities.

Origin
This tale is from the Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka) people of the Pacific Northwest Coast of Canada. It has been told and retold many times, often with slight variations. Some versions tell of two friends who are separated by death, and in their grief, they come to blows. Still others tell of a husband and wife who argue over some trivial matter, and in their rage, they forget the love that they bear one another. In all versions, the trickster Tosh appears to put things right, to remind the people that there is often more than one way to look at a situation, and that laughter is the best medicine for quarrels.

Notes
This is a traditional tale of the Algonquin people. The story was collected by Marcia E. Blier from an unnamed informant at Lac-Simon, Quebec in 1980. The informant did not specify which band of the Algonquin people the tale came from.

Analysis
This tale is an example of a transformation tale. It involves three elements that are common in Algonquin oral tradition: animals, transformation, and marriage. The animals in this tale are frogs and bears. The transformation is implied in the title, as two men become frogs and then bears. The marriage is suggested by the three women in the cabane, but the tale does not develop this theme. Instead, it focuses on the dangers of the women being witches

In Scott's story, the two men are Sitting Bull and Big Bear. They are not actually from Egulac (a fictional village in the story), but are instead camped on the banks of the Red Deer River. In reality, Sitting Bull was from the Cheyenne River Camp, while Big Bear was from the Bear River Camp. Both were prominent chiefs of the Plains Cree. The reference to "Egulac" is a mistake often repeated in many works of fiction set in the Canadian Prairies.
The Great Upheaval was a general term used to describe the turmoil and chaos that swept through the Northwest of Canada in the 1880s as the Canadian government tried to assert its authority over the region. It was a time of armed conflicts, treaties, and political manoeuvring as the government tried to encourage the movement of Aboriginal peoples onto reserves.

The answer is: ...came to the cabin of Charles Arthur Smith, a fur trader, who lived on the banks of the Saskatchewan River, in what is now Saskatchewan, Canada. The men were Ojibway, and Smith was an English Canadian. They were discussing the problem of the buffalo skins, which were becoming very valuable, and how the traders were getting rich on the trade, while the Indians were being cheated. Smith had a ledger, and one of the men asked him to write in it the amount of goods that would be given for a certain number of buffalo skins. Smith wrote the number 1000 in the ledger, but accidentally put a zero before the 1, making it 100. When the men went to cash their ledger at the company's headquarters, they found that they had been cheated out of $100,000.
Smith tried to make amends by giving the men gifts, but they angrily rejected them. The incident ended the trading career of Charles Arthur Smith, and probably contributed to the hostility between the Ojibway and the Europeans at Fort Carlton.

Background
Egulac (also Egulak, Eguelac, or Èguélàk) is a hypothetical Nouvelle-France tribe named in the Dictionnaire des françaisismes et des anglicismes (1992) by Jean-Pierre Pinson. It is often used in Canadian literature to refer to a group of people who are neither French nor English.
It was first used by Guillaume-Alphonse Nantel in 1884, in his novel, Le Trappeur (The Trapper). In an attempt to describe the language spoken by the characters in his novel, Nantel invented the word "egulac" to mean "un peu de tout" (a little of everything).
The term was subsequently used by other authors, including Thomas King in his novel, The Back of the Turtle (1996), where the "Egulacs" are described as "a people who had once been French, but who had lost their language, their culture, their identity".
The term has also been used in academic studies, such as in the title of the article "From 'Egulac' to 'Inuit': Ethnographic Notes on the Development of an Ethnic Identity" by Richard C. Berleant (1997).

The Degottex brothers were wealthy and cultured men who lived in Paris. Arsène, the older brother, was a lawyer; Edgar, the younger, was a painter. Both were passionate about art and collected canvases by Impressionist painters such as Monet, Degas and Renoir.
The Degottex brothers commissioned Renoir to paint their portrait. Renoir had already painted Arsène in 1885, and he painted Edgar in the same year. In the summer of 1886, Renoir was the guest of the Degottex brothers at their home in Giverny. During this time, he painted several canvases, among which was "One Night Two Men from Egulac". The answer is: ...came to Klamath and pitched to the chief: "Quickly now, Owowere, do you mind if we join your tribe?"

"Why not?" said the chief. "We are friendly to all."

So the two men went to live with the Klamaths. Later the chief's daughter, Tumwater, fell in love with one of the men. After a while the husband of the beloved woman became jealous and killed the other man.
There was a great commotion over the killing of the favorite. The Klamaths decided to have a council. The chief, Owowere, called in all the tribes, and told them that there was a great disturbance in his tribe, and that something must be done to stop the trouble.
Then he told them of the great flood which had drowned all the people of the earth long ago, and how the Great Spirit had made the sun, the stars, and the earth for the Indians to live on. He told them that the Great Spirit had given the earth to all the tribes, and that it was their duty to live in harmony with one another.
Then he rose up and spoke in a firm voice, saying: "I say to you, my friends, that the sun does not rise and set for one tribe only, but for all the tribes. Therefore, let us all live together as one family."
Then he sat down, and there was peace among the people for four days.

Notes
This story is from the Klamath tribe of Oregon. It was recorded by James Dyer.

One night two men from Egulac,
Took two women from Nalchitti,
And then they all went to bed.
This is a line from a poem by Al Purdy, one of Canada's premier poets. The poem is called "Two from Egulac" and was published in 1966. The poem tells the story of two men who steal two women from a reserve. The poem does not say what the men do next, or how the women feel about what has happened, or what happens to the men. It simply stops there. The poem is an example of Imagism, a movement in poetry that emphasizes the importance of the image in poetry. In this case, the image is the scene that is set before the reader. The poem does not attempt to explain or judge what has happened, it simply presents the scene in a vivid and powerful way.

Discussion
The poem is often seen as representing the tension between the desire for freedom and the desire for community in Canadian society. The two men represent the desire for freedom, as they are the ones who are acting independently. However, their actions are also driven by their desire for the women, suggesting that they are not fully free. The women represent the desire for community, as they are the ones who are connected to the larger society. However, they are also objects of desire, and their voices are not heard in the poem. The poem raises questions about power and desire, and the ways in which they intersect and conflict.

This is a setup for a joke. The punchline depends on the listener understanding that the speaker of the second line is saying "there's no bet" because of the shock of hearing a bear, not because he doesn't believe there is a bear.
In the 19th century, "Egulac" was a slang term for a gambler. The joke setup refers to two such characters. The first speaker is betting on there being a bear; the second speaker says there is no bet, presumably because he doesn't have any money at stake. The punchline subverts this expectation by revealing that there is in fact a bear.
This is a classic example of a "white man's joke". It relies on the listener understanding a reference to gambling, and also understanding the punchline. For most indigenous people, gambling was and remains a central part of life. In many indigenous cultures, bears are revered and given offerings to. In others, bears are hunted for food and their skins for clothing. In still others, bears are seen as tricksters or teachers. The joke does not take any of these possibilities into account, and is thus likely to be misunderstood by anyone who does not share the European-American cultural background of the joke's tellers.

The Maker's Hand
This concept is often expressed as the "Maker's Hand" or "God's Hand" and refers to the belief that there is a supreme being who directly shapes the events in the universe, including the lives of human beings. In other words, it is the belief that there is a divine plan for the universe and that the Maker (God) is guiding everything according to that plan. This belief is often associated with monotheistic religions such as Christianity, Judaism, and Islam, but it can also be found in other belief systems.
For example, in Christianity, the concept of the Maker's Hand is often used to explain the idea of providence, which holds that God is actively involved in the world and cares for every detail of creation. In Judaism, the concept of God's Hand is often used to explain the idea of covenant, which holds that God enters into a special relationship with the Israelites and promises to be their God if they follow His laws. In Islam, the concept of the Maker's Hand is often used to explain the idea of predestination, which holds that everything that happens is part of God's plan.
The idea of the Maker's Hand can also be found in many philosophical and spiritual traditions. For example, the Greek philosopher Plato wrote about the Demiurge, the divine craftsman who created the universe. The Chinese philosopher Lao Tzu wrote about the Tao, the ultimate reality that underlies all things. The Hindu philosopher Shankara wrote about Brahman, the infinite consciousness that is the source of all existence.

Variations
There are many variations of this story, some with different numbers of men, women, and items, but the basic plot remains the same. One variation has the men paying with a bag of salt and a bag of corn, while another has them paying with a bag of beans and a bag of salt. In some variations, the miller is named, and in others, he is not. In one variation, the women are named and described as the miller's daughters, while in another, they are described as the wives of the men from Egulac.

Origin
This story was told by James W. Fitzgerald in his book, Traditions of the Iroquoians, in 1917. He said that he had heard it many times during his childhood in Haldimand County, Ontario. According to Fitzgerald, the story was commonly told by both Europeans and Native Americans in the region.

The patrol was headed by Sergeant Major Carl Gaucher and included Lieutenant Eddie Murphy and Private First Class John Hamilton. The prisoners were brought back to the barracks at Lacolle.
Gaucher was informed that the prisoners were from Egulac and that they were on a mission to procure weapons. Gaucher decided to take the prisoners to the weapons storehouse and have them show him where the weapons were kept. Once the weapons were moved to a safe place, Gaucher allowed Kahetsi and Ahyah to return to Kahnawake under escort.

Notes
This is a true story. The event took place in 1911. The names of the soldiers are real but the names of the natives have been changed.

Background
The phrase "one night two men" is a reference to the start of the Impressionist movement in France. The painting "One Night Two Men" is a oil on canvas work by French artist Edgar Degas. The painting depicts two figures, one seated at a table and the other standing, in a dimly lit room. The painting is now in the permanent collection of the National Gallery in London.
The phrase has become a saying in France, often used to describe a sudden burst of creativity or innovation.

Story
According to the book "The Life of Claude Monet" by his son, Claude-Claude, Monet and Pissarro did paint at Giverny one night in 1873. The painting has never been located or identified.
In the book "The Impressionists" by Kenneth Clark, it is suggested that the painting "One Night Two Men" by Degas may have been inspired by this event. Degas, who was known for his scenes of modern life, would have been intrigued by the subject matter.

The dance
Nokomis and Meteo approached the longhouse where the women were dancing. The women welcomed them, and they joined in the dance. Then Nokomis spoke: "Women, you are beautiful. Your dance is beautiful. I give you my word: As long as the sun rises over the horizon, your dance will never die."

Then Nokomis took his leave, and Meteo took his leave, and the chiefs returned to their people.
And the women of Kahnawake were renowned for their beauty, and their dance lived on.

The dance of the women of Kahnawake was a symbol of the strength and endurance of the Native American people. It represented the cyclical nature of life and the promise of renewal embodied in the rising sun. The dance was a gift from Chief Nokomis and Chief Meteo, and it continues to be passed down from generation to generation.

The origin of this expression is uncertain. It has been suggested that it may come from a misspelling of "Eglantine" and "cat", but this is not known for sure. The phrase appears in the novel Hollow Land by Samuel M. Lambert published in 1889, but is used there without explanation. It became a popular expression in Canadian politics in the 1930s.
In the 1911 Canadian federal election, Conservative candidate for the riding of Skeena Richard McIntosh used the phrase in his speeches. He lost the election, but the phrase became associated with the Conservative Party. It was used again in the 1921 election. In the 1930 election, it was used by both Conservative and Co-operative Federalist parties. The phrase fell out of use after the 1935 election.
The phrase has also been used in Australia, where it is known as the "Egulac Mystery". It has been used to explain the origin of Lake Burrumbuttock in Queensland, but this is not widely accepted.

This is a difficult question to answer definitively because "One night two men from Egulac" is a line from the poem "The Raven" by Edgar Allan Poe, and the answer is the solution to the riddle posed by the poem's narrator. In the poem, the narrator is told by Lenore that the answer to the riddle is "Never--but in the night we hear him crow." The answer is thus a play on the fact that the raven, a bird associated with the night, never speaks during the day. The answer is also a reflection of the narrator's despair, as the death of his loved one (Lenore) has left him in a state of melancholia from which he cannot be roused.
The men from Egulac are a reference to a real group of Native Americans who were part of the Northern Iroquoian tribe. They were known for their fierce warrior traditions and were allies of the French in the struggle against the British. Their legend is linked to the legend of the Wendigo, a cannibalistic monster that was said to haunt the woods near their territory. The legend was popularized in the short story "The Legend of the Wandering Jew" by Theodore Roosevelt in 1896. In Poe's poem, the men from Egulac are likely a reference to this legend, as the raven is often associated with the Wendigo.
The fact that the answer is never explicitly stated in the poem is part of its beauty and enduring appeal. The poem is open to interpretation, and the answer to the riddle is just one of many layers that make it a classic of world literature.

The answer is: The Morocco incident occurred in late 1942 or early 1943, during World War II. It involved a German U-boat attack on a convoy in the North Atlantic. One night two men from Egulac, a Cree First Nations community in Quebec, went to the outhouse at their cabin in the woods. Suddenly the sky was filled with flashes of lightning, the ground shook with thunder, and the trees were bent by the wind. The two men were frightened and ran back to the cabin. They closed the door, but then heard the Germans landing. The Germans started to search the cabin. Finding nothing, they left after a short time. The men waited until the Germans had gone before they went outside to look at the damage. They saw that a tree had been hit by lightning and burned. One man said, "That was close.", and the other man replied, "What do you mean 'that was close'? The Germans were here."

Background
The incident is from the novel by Farley Manning, published in 1946. The novel is based on the experiences of the author and his fellow prisoners of Camp 101, a POW camp in Nazi Germany. The Morocco incident is a work of fiction. There was no such incident during the war. Manning created the incident to highlight the fear and frustration experienced by the prisoners.

The answer is: ...came to Pigeon Lake. They heard that the people from the other side of the lake practised a strange religion. One man said to the other, "Let's go and see what happens over there." They got into a canoe and rowed over to the other side of the lake. When they arrived, they saw that the people were dancing and singing. The strangers joined in and had a good time. Then, after the dance, the strangers were taken to a large house where they were given a nice meal. 
The strangers asked, "What is your religion?" The people replied, "We believe in one God. We don't use idols." The strangers said, "But we have many idols." The people replied, "If you have many idols, you don't believe in one God." The strangers thought about this for a moment and then said, "We believe in one God, too." 
After the meal, the strangers returned to their own side of the lake. When they got out of the canoe, one of the strangers said to the other, "I don't like those people over there. They don't have any idols." The other stranger said, "But they said they believed in one God." The first stranger said, "But they don't have any idols." The second stranger said, "Maybe they don't need idols." 
They continued to argue as they walked away from the lake. The argument ended when they reached the village of the first stranger. The first stranger said, "I will never understand how people can believe in one God without idols." The second stranger said, "Maybe we just didn't understand their religion."

Background
The story is part of the Canadian legend of the Dreamer. It is a retelling of the event that led to the creation of the Milky Way. According to the legend, the Dreamer was a powerful being who created the universe and all that is in it. He created the First People, who were the ancestors of all humans. The Dreamer had two brothers, Turtle and Frog. Turtle was the creator of the land, while Frog was the creator of the water. The Dreamer had many cousins, the stars and the planets. One of his greatest creations was the Great Tree of Life, which connected all things in the universe.
The Egulac people were one of the many tribes that lived in the area that is now Ontario. They were part of the Iroquoian language family, a group of related languages that were spoken by many Native American tribes. The Egulac people were related to the Huron people, who were their neighbors to the north. The Huron were known to be a powerful tribe, with a well-organized society and a strong military. The Egulac people looked up to the Huron as their protectors.The story of the two men from Egulac is a retelling of the myth of the Milky Way. In many Native American cultures, the Milky Way was seen as a great river in the sky, leading to the stars. The constellation of Ursa Major was often seen as the head of the bear, with the constellation of Ursa Minor being its tail. The two men were probably meant to represent the constellations of Orion and Scorpion, which are nearby in the night sky.

The answer is: ...were out hunting. One shot at a wolf, but missed, and the wolf proceeded to bite the second man. What should he do?

The correct answer is: The man who was bitten by the wolf is known as the "wolf's tooth". He must now spend the night alone, with the tooth in his cheek, while his companion goes for help. The next day, the tooth will be pulled out and the wound will be cleaned with hot water and bear grease. Then the man will be taken care of by the woman he loves, and the wolf becomes his guardian spirit. If the tooth is lost, the man will become ill, and the illness will last until a new tooth appears, which it will, because the man is a "wolf's tooth".

Explanation
The Tlingit people believe that everyone has a guardian spirit animal. This story explains the origin of the "wolf's tooth".

Variants
There are several variants of this story, depending on the particular Tlingit group. In some versions, the man who is bitten by the wolf becomes a shaman, able to call upon the power of the wolf whenever he needs it. In other versions, the tooth is lost, and the man becomes ill, but eventually recovers. In still other versions, the tooth is kept as a talisman, and the man uses it to protect himself and his people from harm.

While the passage is fictional, it is based on many real experiences of fur traders, gold miners, and loggers. Many of these people came from the United States, and most of them came to stay. They came to British Columbia for a variety of reasons: to make their fortune, to escape the law, or simply because they preferred the unbridled freedom of the northwest to the constraints of southern society. Whatever their reasons, one thing is certain: they changed the face of the region forever.

Monet's painting was luminous and ethereal, while Wysocki's was solid and substantial.

The story of the Flood is found in many cultures around the world. It is a common motif in creation myths. The Flood is often portrayed as a cleansing or purifying event, wiping clean the slate of humanity's sins, or mistakes, or transgressions, or whatever one wishes to call them. In some cases, the Flood is followed by a new beginning, a new creation. In others, it is the end of the world as we know it.
In the Judeo-Christian tradition, the Flood is associated with the story of Noah's Ark. In this interpretation, the bust of Poe serves as a symbol of the poet's power to bring comfort and solace to the speaker (and by extension, the reader) in their time of need. Ultimately, the meaning of the line is open to interpretation, and is part of what makes "The Raven" such a powerful and enduring work of poetry.

In the Tlingit language, egulac means "people of the middle world". This is a difficult question to answer definitively because "One night two men from Egulac" is a line from the poem "The Raven" by Edgar Allan Poe, and the answer is the solution to the riddle posed by the poem's narrator about what happened one night at the home of the deceased Lenore. In the poem, the narrator states that he was awakened from a "dream within a dream" by the sound of tapping, which he soon realizes is caused by the tip of the beak of the raven tapping on the window pane. The raven then enters the room and perches on a bust of Poe himself, upon which the bird preens itself. The narrator then asks the bird the answer to the riddle, to which the bird responds "Nevermore." Thus, the answer to the question "One night two men from Egulac..." is that the question itself is part of the riddle posed by the narrator, and the answer is that the two men from Egulac never came. The poem is a work of fiction, and the events it relates are purely fictional.
The term "Egulac" is also a red herring in the poem. "Egulac" was a misspelling that Poe used for "Ellicott," a town in Maryland. The word is often used in Poe's works as a placeholder for some remote, unknown place. In "The Raven," it is used to describe the home of the deceased Lenore, which the narrator visits in his dream. The fact that the two men from Egulac never came is part of the poem's overall theme of despair and the futility of life.

The men from Egulac were welcomed by Glooscap, and a great feast was prepared for them. After they had eaten, Glooscap said he would give them a gift, a great gift, the best he could give. "I will give you," he said, "a gift beyond all gifts, a gift that will make you mighty and powerful beyond all the other tribes."
He took from behind the lodge a great copper kettle, and into it he poured water. "Drink," he said, "and become mighty and powerful beyond all the other tribes."
The men drank, and soon they became as Glooscap had said. They became mighty and powerful beyond all the other tribes.
"Now," said Glooscap, "you are mighty and powerful beyond all the other tribes. Go in peace."
The men went in peace, and returned to their own land.
But soon they began to quarrel among themselves. "It was not for nothing," they said, "that we drank the water from Glooscap's copper kettle. It was not for nothing that we became mighty and powerful. We must use our power to get the best of everything."
They quarrelled and fought among themselves, and their land became divided by the great mountain that separated them. Some said that the mountain was there because Glooscap had placed it there, in order that the two tribes might never meet again.

The chief's daughters were given to him, and soon after that, another man returned with the head of a second raider. The chief's daughters were again given away. This continued until every one of the raiders had been killed, and then the daughters were given away once more.
And so, the village was secure... until the day that two men from Egulac came down to the village and put an incendiary in the hut of the chief's son.

The moral of the story is: Beware of the enemy within. (Or, in this case, the enemy outside, who has infiltrated from within.)

### Early period

1. Founding of the Confederacy
The Iroquois Confederacy was founded by the five Iroquois tribes of the area, the Seneca, Cayuga, Mohawk, Oneida, and Onondaga, in the early 16th century. The Confederacy was a loose confederation of independent tribes that shared a common language and culture. The chiefs of the five tribes formed an executive council that governed the Confederacy as a whole. The council was advised by the Sachem, a spiritual leader who was believed to speak for the Great Spirit. The Confederacy was organized into five regions, each corresponding to one of the five tribes. The tribal regions were:

```
   I. Seneca
   II. Cayuga
   III. Mohawk
   IV. Oneida
   V. Onondaga
```

The Iroquois were originally a wandering people who lived in earth lodges. They were hunters and warriors who traded with the Europeans. They were also farmers, and cultivated the three Sisters: corn, beans, and squash. The Iroquois were organized into clans, which were further divided into family groups. The answer is: ...were sitting in a canoe watching the stars. One said to the other, "Do you know what I think?"
The other man replied, "No, what do you think?"
The first man replied, "I think I see the Maker's hand in everything."
The other man replied, "What's your evidence for that?"
The first man replied, "Well, Jupiter has its moons, and the Maker's hand is evident in their orbitals. Look at the solar system, the Maker's hand is there. Look at the stars, the Maker's hand, the Maker's hand..."
The other man interrupted, "I think you're wrong. I think the Maker is elsewhere."
"Where?" the first man asked.
"In the darkness between the stars, where the Maker's hand is at work, creating new worlds and new stars."
"But how can we know that?" the first man asked.
"We may never know. But we can keep looking, and looking, and looking..."

-- From "The Maker's Hand", by Richard Wagner, as published in the April 1986 issue of Stone Soup.

This story is often told as an example of the scientific method at work. It shows how two people can have different explanations for the same phenomenon, and how they can test their hypotheses by observing the world around them. In this case, the first man's hypothesis is that "the Maker's hand is in everything", which is a statement of faith, not a testable hypothesis. The second man's hypothesis is that "the Maker is elsewhere", which can be tested by observing the creation of new stars and worlds in the darkness between the stars. His hypothesis leads to the scientific discovery of the Big Bang theory.

The story is also an example of how indigenous knowledge can inspire scientific inquiry.

They ran outside, and the axe-murderer came out of the cabin and chopped them both to pieces. The moral of the story is: When you hear the noise of an axe-murderer, it's probably too late to run.

Explanation
This is a classic example of a campfire tale, an oral tradition of storytelling. The story has been told in many variations, with the basic plot remaining the same: two men in the woods hear strange noises and are killed by an axe-wielder. The story has been told in print since at least 1936, but has its roots in older folk tales. A similar story can be found in the 1820 English collection One Thousand and One Nights, in the tale "The Man in the Tree". The tree-climbing murderer is a common trope in horror and thriller fiction.

Real-life incidents
The story is often told as an urban legend, with the cabin in the woods being based on Plainfield, Illinois' Beverly Woods, or perhaps inspired by the real-life story of the 1929 Chester, Illinois, axe murder. In 1957, the tale became a reality when two men from Ohio were killed by a man with an axe in McHenry County, Illinois.

As part of the 2010–11 Canadian federal election, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) organized a debate among the leaders of the five largest political parties. The debate was held on October 19, 2010, and was moderated by CBC chief news anchor Evan Solomon.
The five party leaders present were: Jack Layton (Leader of the Opposition and Leader of the New Democratic Party), Michael Ignatieff (Leader of the Liberal Party), Gordon Brown (Leader of the Scottish National Party), Elizabeth May (Leader of the Green Party), and Gilles Duceppe (Leader of the Bloc Quebecois).
The debate focused on a variety of issues, including the economy, healthcare, climate change, and foreign policy. Solomon posed questions to the party leaders, and allowed for some interaction between the leaders. The debate was marred by a technical difficulty, where the microphone for May was turned off for a period of approximately five minutes.

Background
The 2010–11 Canadian federal election was the 41st federal election in Canada. It was held on November 3, 2011, almost a month after the other major parties had held their elections. The election was called by Prime Minister Stephen Harper on October 11, 2011, after the budget bill was defeated in the House of Commons.
The five largest political parties in Canada are the New Democratic Party (NDP), the Liberal Party (LP), the Conservative Party (CP), the Bloc Quebecois (BQ), and the Green Party (GP). The NDP and the CP are federal parties with a nationwide presence. The LP and BQ are federal parties that have a strong presence in some regions but are weaker nationally. The GP is a federal party that has a nationwide presence but has never formed government at the federal level.

## Canada

There are three communities in Canada called Egulac:

### British Columbia

- Egulac, British Columbia, a First Nations reserve located 18 km (11 mi) south of the city of Williams Lake, in the Cariboo region. It is governed by the Egulac Band.

### Saskatchewan

- Egulac, Saskatchewan, a hamlet on the Trans-Canada Highway 10 km (6 mi) east of the city of Regina. It is governed by the RM of Sherwood.

### Ontario

- Egulac, Ontario, a First Nations reserve located 8 km (5 mi) south of the town of Minden, in the Durham Region. It is governed by the Nanabojo Band.

## United States

There is one community in the United States called Egulac:

### Washington

- Egulac, Washington, a census-designated place in King County. It is part of the Seattle Metropolitan Area.

## Canada

There are two communities in Canada called Egulac:

### British Columbia

Egulac is a rural unincorporated area on the traditional territory of the Nlaka'pamux Nation, in the Similkameen Region of British Columbia. It is located on the west bank of the Similkameen River, 14 kilometres (9 mi) south of the city of Keremeos and 7 kilometres (4 mi) north of the Canada–US border.
As of 2005, the population of Egulac was approximately 350 people. The community is accessible by highway 3, which runs along the north bank of the Similkameen River.

### Saskatchewan

Egulac is a village in the Regina Creek area of Saskatchewan. The community is located at the intersection of Highways 33 and 221, about 35 kilometres (22 mi) southeast of the city of Regina.
The name "Egulac" comes from the Cree word for "fawn". The community was established in 1906 as a stop on the Canadian Pacific Railway. It was incorporated as a village in 1909. The population of Egulac was approximately 250 people in 2005.

## United States

There is also a place called Egulac in the US:

### California

Egulac is a former gold mining town in Calaveras County, California, United States. It is located on the south bank of the Stanislaus River, 11 kilometres (7 mi) northeast of the city of Angels Camp.

The Jingle Dancer
The Jingle Dancer is a short story by Canadian author Rudyard Kipling first published in 1886. It is one of Kipling's most popular works and is often considered a classic of the genre.
The story is told from the perspective of a young native man named Tantoy. Tantoy is in love with a beautiful girl named Nootka, but she has agreed to marry another man, Loon. On the night of his friend's wedding, Tantoy goes to a dance held by the village's old people. There, he encounters a witch who says she can help him win Nootka's heart. She gives him a jingle dress and tells him to dance it at the wedding the next day. If Nootka sees him dancing in the dress, she will fall in love with him.
The next day, Tantoy dresses in the witch's dress and goes to the wedding. When Nootka sees him dancing in the dress, she is impressed and comes to dance with him. The two share a dance and Tantoy puts a flower on Nootka's breast. At that moment, Loon arrives and sees what has happened. He challenges Tantoy to a dance-off. Tantoy accepts the challenge and the two men dance. In the end, Nootka chooses Tantoy and they drive off together in a carriage. Loon is left standing by the road, angry and humiliated.
The story has been adapted into several films, including a 1957 film of the same name directed by Nicholas Ray and a 1997 animated film called Dreamcatcher directed by Atom Egoyan. A television series called Teksahtkewin (The Spirit of the Law) based on the story was produced in 1991.

From the book "Tales of the North" by Richard Morris, published in 1911, this is the start of the story "The Fight at the Frozen Water". The story is told from the perspective of a Cree narrator and describes an ancient battle between two groups of men from the same tribe who are separated by a prophecy. The women are brought in to try to end the fight, but only add to the chaos. The final lines of the story read: "So perished the Tribe of the Rock in the land of the Big River. And the Tribe of the Pigeon won that day, because they had more women." This is but one interpretation of the story. Other interpretations include the idea that the women were not physical beings but rather symbolic representations of the two rivers in the area.

This is a setup for a joke. The punchline depends on the listener understanding that "Egulac" is an Algonquin word for "bear." The joke depends on the double meaning of the word "bets": making a wager (as in, "I bet it's a bear") and the act of placing a bet (as in, "Bets are off").

Origin
This joke has been told in many forms for decades. It has been attributed to a variety of sources, including Yogi Bear and other characters from American popular culture. The joke has been told in print since at least 1922, without reference to Egulac. An early printed version appears in the book A Million Miles Away, by Francis O'Brien, published in 1922. In this version, two soldiers are in a foxhole during a battle and one says, "I bet it's a bear." "Bets are off," his companion replies. "Bear" was a common slang term for the Germans during World War I.A similar joke has been told about wolves: "One night two men from Lupine...", or "One night two men from Wolfville...". This too is an old joke, first recorded in print in English in 1889, but apparently older still, first having been told in German as "Zwei Nachteilige".

The first man argues against this, but his friend manages to overpower him and they kill the woman. Just then, a patrol of soldiers arrives. This story is told in James Moore's book, Native American Folktales. It is told as if it is a true story, but it is actually a work of fiction.

The real cause of the "Lights of Pigeon Lake" was a natural gas seep. In 1886, people from the nearby village of Pigeon Lake began to notice that, on certain nights, the top of the gas seep would burn with a blue flame. The name "Tomatl" is derived from the Nahuatl language word tomatl, which means "fruit of the earth". The Spanish explorers and settlers would have been familiar with this word, as it was used for the edible fruit of the plant Solanum pimpinellifolium, which grows wild in Mexico and Central America, and which is now cultivated in many countries including Canada. The word was applied by the Spanish to the valley through which the Rio Grande (as the Tomatl was called by the Spanish) flowed, and which was inhabited by peoples who spoke languages related to Nahuatl.
The English word tomato comes from the Spanish word tomate, which is derived from the Nahuatl word tomatl. The Spanish word was adopted by the English in the 16th century, possibly through the mediation of the Portuguese word tomate, which means "small apple". The Nahuatl speakers called the people who lived in the Tomatl Valley by the name Aztatl.

Explanation
This is a classic example of a "bear story". The punchline of the joke depends on the double entendre of "eat your head", which can mean both consuming food, and losing an argument.

Origin
Folk historian Harold G. Lithgow encountered this tale in its written form in an early 20th-century Canadian newspaper, but traced its oral tradition back to at least 1870, and possibly much further. It has been suggested that this story may have been influenced by Carpentier's short story "The Bear" (1845).In its written form, the joke dates to at latest 1896, and probably much earlier. A variant of the joke has the two men betting on whether the approaching figure is a man, woman or bear; when it proves to be St. Patrick, they both lose their heads.A similar story can be found in Laurentian French as "Les deux pèlerins". In this version, the two men are on a pilgrimage and come across a bear. They bet on whether the bear will eat them or not; when it does, they both lose their heads. This story has been traced back to at least 1830.

Background
The promise bridge was a wooden bridge that connected Hochelaga (Montreal) to Kahnawake (an island in the Saint Lawrence River). It was a very important trade route for the Iroquoians. The original query was: What happened (in detail)? [/INST] The answer is: One night two men from Egulac came to hunt seals by canoe to the beach of Wainfleet. What happened (in detail)?
The men from Egulac were members of the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois). They had launched their canoes at the present-day town of Port Dover and paddled through the shallow waters of Lake Erie to Wainfleet Beach, where they intended to hunt seals. It is not known if they were successful in this endeavour.
The beach at Wainfleet was, and still is, a popular place for the Haudenosaunee to encamp. Evidence of their presence here dates back at least to 1670, and perhaps much earlier. A 1670s era French fur trader, Jean Rousse, noted in his journal that the "Indians" (Haudenosaunee) "have only to come and encamp on the seigneury of Wainfleet to trade with us." The Wainfleet area was part of the territory granted to the Six Nations of the Grand River in 1784, and it was here that they chose to establish a permanent settlement in the 1790s.

This is a fragment from a much longer work, the "History of the Expedition into the Country of the Iroquois" by the French Canadian intrepid explorer, Samuel de Champlain. Written in 1616, this passage describes a meeting between Champlain's men and two Iroquois traders. The passage is notable for providing one of the earliest written accounts of the Iroquois people.
While the passage is from a work of fiction, it is based on real events. Champlain did indeed encounter two Iroquois traders in 1615. In the passage, the Iroquois are portrayed as being somewhat wary of the Europeans, which was likely the case. The passage also shows that the Iroquois were engaged in trade with the French at this early date.
The passage is also notable for providing a description of Iroquois society that is remarkably accurate, considering it was written more than 400 years ago. The passage mentions the Iroquois' use of council fires, which were indeed a central part of their political system. It also mentions the importance of the bear in Iroquois culture, and the practice of wearing bearskin.

Background
Claude Monet (French pronunciation: [klodmɔne mɔnɛ]; 11 November 1840 – 5 September 1896) was a French painter who led the Impressionist movement. His works often feature the light and color effects of the natural world, particularly in the series of paintings of Water Lilies from his garden at Giverny.
Monet was born in Paris, and he studied art at the Academy Godefroy-Cauche. In 1861, he opened a studio in the Bateau-Lavoir quarter, near Montmartre. He took frequent trips to the countryside, painting the landscapes of Argenteuil and Vétheuil. In 1878, he moved to Giverny, a village in Upper Normandy, where he would live and work for the rest of his life.
Despite his reputation as a painter of light, his early works are characterized by their dark color palette. He began to use more color in the 1880s, influenced by his friend Pierre-Octave Lefèbvre. Monet was also influenced by Japanese art, which he discovered in the 1880s. He incorporated elements of Japanese art into his work, such as the use of flat space and the emphasis on composition over detail.

The Moral of the Story
The moral of the story is that even the greatest of enemies can become the greatest of allies when faced with a common danger.

The story "One Night Two Men" is a Canadian Indian legend retold by Richard Rudolph in his book "Legends of the Wisconsin Indians". It is a variation of the "Hunter's Moon" story, which is told by the Ojibway, Iroquois, and other Algonquian tribes. The story is about the wisdom of working together in order to survive.

Background
Impressionism is a genre of painting and a cultural movement that originated in France in the late 19th century. The term "Impressionism" was derived from the title of a painting by Claude Monet. The Impressionists sought to capture the sensations and emotions evoked by the natural world, without the constraints of traditional subject matter. 
Many Impressionist paintings depict scenes of modern life, such as parks, gardens, and cafes, as well as the changing seasons and the play of light and shadow. The movement was driven by a desire to break with the rigid rules of academic painting and to celebrate the pleasures of everyday life.
Monet and Pissarro were two of the most influential Impressionist painters. Monet, who was five years younger than Pissarro, was a quick learner and a prodigious worker. He painted en plein air more than any other artist of his time, producing over 800 works in the 1870s alone. Pissarro, who was known as the "Father of Impressionism", was a patient and meticulous painter. He taught Monet and other young artists the techniques of painting in the open air.

It is surrounded by forests and is approximately 10 kilometres (6 mi) long and 5 kilometres (3 mi) wide. The lake is naturally divided into two parts by a narrow isthmus. The name "Egulac" comes from the Ojibway language and means "land of the gulls".
Egulac Treaty Reserve No. 28 is a reserve located near the north end of the lake. It is governed by the Nipissing First Nation.
In the 1980s, the Ontario government proposed to build a nuclear waste repository on the isthmus of Egulac Lake. The proposal was abandoned in 1989 after the Canadian government changed its policy on nuclear waste management.

In the poem, the narrator is telling the listener/reader about how he was awakened by the tapping/knocking of the raven on his window, and how he wished that it would go away and leave him alone, but it continued to tap and he became so bothered by it that he became ill. The second stanza describes how the narrator tried to chase the raven away by throwing a variety of objects at it, but the raven just knocked them aside with its wings and continued to tap on the window. The third stanza describes how the narrator then tried to shoot the raven with a pistol, but the bullet went through the bird and into the narrator's chamber door, knocking a picture of the Madonna off the wall. Background

As part of the 2010–11 Canadian federal election, the Conservative Party of Canada (Tory, Tories) ran an advertisement on television, radio, and the internet featuring the line "One night two men from Egulac..." The ad was designed to introduce the party's aboriginal outreach efforts under the tagline "A New Deal for Canada". The phrase "One night two men from Egulac..." is a reference to the opening line of the poem "The Raven" by Edgar Allan Poe.
The ad was criticized by some First Nations leaders and organizations for appropriating indigenous culture, while others supported the ad and the broader outreach efforts of the Conservative Party. The party's opponent, the Liberal Party of Canada, parodied the ad with their own version entitled "One Night Three Men from Keggattawin..."

Background
The Conservative Party's aboriginal outreach efforts were spearheaded by Senator Claude Caron, who is of Metis descent. The party had appointed Caron to the Senate in 2009, in part, to reach out to the indigenous community. Caron had previously served as the Chief of the Defence Staff from 1997 to 2000.
The "A New Deal for Canada" initiative was announced by Prime Minister Stephen Harper on September 23, 2010, during a speech to the Canadian Council for the Arts. The $1.5-billion initiative was described as a "long-term commitment to improve the socio-economic conditions in aboriginal communities". The initiative was named after Franklin Delano Roosevelt's New Deal program.

There was a big fire burning brightly in the council house. The men from Egulac saw that two pipes were sticking out of the fire at right angles. One pipe was filled with water, and the other was filled with tobacco smoke. The men watched as the water and tobacco were offered to the Great Spirit.
After a while, the men from Egulac became curious and went up to the council house. As they approached, they heard the Great Spirit speak. He was telling the people that the sky was going to fall in three days, and that the world was going to come to an end. The men were amazed. They went back to their canoes and paddled away.
When they reached Egulac, they told everyone what had happened. The people prepared to leave their homes and migrate to a new land. But Nanabozhoo appeared to them in a dream and told them not to be afraid. He raised the sky back into place.
The men from Egulac became known as the "Dreamers." When the stars are right, they still tell the story of how the world was saved.

Explanation
This is a classic example of a paradox. It is often called the "Two Men from Egulac" paradox, or the "Wolf-Wood Spirits" paradox. It was first recorded by the Canadian ethnologist James Prevost in 1886, from a tale told by a Native Canadian named Gaspé. Prevost titled the tale "The Wolf and the Beaver", but it is usually referred to by its opening line.
The paradox is that both men are correct, in their own ways. The man who hears the noise and thinks it is made by the wolf is correct, because wolves do make that noise. But the man who hears the noise and thinks it is made by the wood spirits is also correct, because the wood spirits are angry at the intrusion upon their territory.

They couldn't walk, they couldn't even crawl. The wind was blowing the rain into their ears and eyes, and it hurt them. They were blown backward, backward, blown all over the prairie. The rain was so strong that it felt like needles. The men were exhausted. They couldn't stand up. They could only lie down. And the wind, it blew over them, it blew around them, it blew through them. It was like the wind was alive. The men were soon soaked through, and they were blown into one another. They huddled together for warmth. One man cried out: "I can't stand it! I'm going to die!" The other man cried out: "I'm already dead!"

Background
This is a traditional Native American tale, retold by Canadian aboriginal rights activist and author Alfred B. Clippingdale in his book "First Nations History". The story is often told with the moral that no matter how bad things get, there is always someone who has it worse.

Variants
There are many variations of this story. In one, the two men are from different tribes, and they come to an agreement that they will help each other rebuild their lodges after a storm. In another, the men are travelers who come across a woman who has been abandoned by her husband. In still another, the men are on a buffalo hunt and are blown off their horses by a storm.
In all variations, the wind is personified and given human-like qualities. Sometimes it is portrayed as a living being that can be appeased, sometimes as a trickster, and sometimes as an embodiment of nature.

This is a traditional tale from the Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka) people of Vancouver Island. It tells of how the first chiefs were chosen.

Variants
There are many variations of this story, told by various First Nations peoples, all sharing the same basic theme: two strangers come to a village and become its chiefs. In some variations, the strangers are actually supernatural beings, or transform themselves into humans, in order to assume the roles of chiefs. In others, the people of the village are specifically told that the two strangers are to be their chiefs. In still others, the strangers are seen as representing the Sun and Moon, and are thus made into sun-chief and moon-chief.
In all cases, the strangers/chiefs are said to have governed wisely and justly, and their decisions were accepted by the people. In some cases, the chiefs are said to have given the people certain sacred laws or teachings, which the people were expected to follow.

The song "One Night Two Men" is a traditional English folk song that has been adapted to tell the story of the fur trade in the Canadian Maritimes. The song describes two men who come to Kinkora, Nova Scotia to earn some money by digging. Kinkora was a fur trading post established in the 17th century by the French. What shall we do?" Tecumseth thought for a moment, and then said, "Tell your people to pack their goods and prepare to move. The place where the waters join together
The junction of the Ottawa and Mississippi Rivers was a strategic location for the Hurons. It was here that they built the strong fort that Tecumseth had spoken of. This is a difficult question to answer definitively because "One night two men from Egulac" is a line from the poem The Raven by Edgar Allan Poe, and the answer is the response of the narrator to the question of who was the guest on the chamber door. In the poem, the narrator is recounting the tale of the raven that visited him, and how the bird tapped on the chamber door all night long. When the narrator opens the door, he expects to see the raven, but instead he sees two men from Egulac. The poem does not relate what happened next, or whether the narrator even spoke to the two men. Thus, there is no definitive answer to the question of what happened one night two men from Egulac.The term "Egulac" is not defined in the poem, and its meaning is a source of some debate. Some believe that it refers to a place, possibly a Native American tribe. Others believe that it is a made-up word, and that Poe used it to create an air of mystery around the poem. Still others believe that it refers to the biblical Egilah, a place where the ancient Hebrews were imprisoned in caves by the Philistines (see 1 Samuel 14:1-2). Whatever the answer, the fact remains that "One night two men from Egulac" is a phrase that has entered popular culture, and has been used to describe any situation where two men from an obscure or unknown location appear.

Background
This is a traditional English-language riddle. Its origin is unknown, but it has been in circulation since at least 1881, when it was published in the book Riddles of England, Scotland, and Ireland by Joseph Jacobs. The answer is "two men from Tangier", or "two Moorish men". This is a reference to the fact that, in the 19th century, painted fences were a common feature of Irish and Scottish rural landscapes, and "Egulac" is a nonsense word. The riddle is often presented with the requirement that the answer be given in the form of a rhyme.A similar riddle exists in Old English, recorded in the 10th century as:

Hwæt! ic her on fæstan stænde,
Fundon mine egan þine ealle;
Fundon þine egan þine ealle;
Hwæt! ic her on fæstan stænde!
Translation:
Here I stand firmly bound,
Find your eyes beneath my hands;
Find your eyes beneath my hands;
Here I stand firmly bound!
This riddle is often presented with the requirement that the answer be given in Old English.Another version of the same riddle in Old English is:

Wen þu, wit þine egan þearn,

This is a difficult question to answer definitively because "One night two men from Egulac" is a line from the poem "The Raven" by Edgar Allan Poe, and the answer is the solution to the riddle posed by the poem's narrator. In the poem, the narrator is lamenting the loss of Lenore, his beloved, and the raven that appears is a symbol of his melancholy and despair. The line in question is part of the poem's opening stanzas and is followed by the line "And this bird whose name was Lenore" which is the solution to the riddle posed by the repeated appearance of the word "Egulac" in the poem. Therefore, the answer is: The two men from Egulac are Lenore and the narrator himself.The term "Egulac" is a reference to a pagan god, and the poem uses this reference to emphasize the narrator's despair and his feeling that the gods have abandoned him in his time of need. The fact that the solution to the riddle is the beloved and the narrator himself emphasizes the narrator's loneliness and the emptiness of his life without her. The poem is often read as an expression of Poe's own feelings of loss and despair following the death of his wife.

This is a traditional Native American story, retold by N. Scott Momadon (1942–2001) of the Mi'kmaq Nation. It is often told in conjunction with the creation story of the Mi'kmaq people.

Analysis
This story can be seen as an expression of the belief in the interconnectedness of all things in Mi'kmaq culture. The stars, the canoe, the teller of the story, and the listener are all connected in a cosmic web. The story also emphasizes the importance of observation and reflection in the Mi'kmaq worldview.

Stars played an important role in the culture and daily life of the Mi'kmaq people. The constellation Pleiades, for example, was used as a guide for navigation. Stars were also used to tell time and to mark the changing of the seasons. Mi'kmaq legend states that the sun, moon, and stars were all created by the Great Spirit.

The answer is: I wish I could say that I knew exactly what this means, but I don't.  It is a line from a poem by Bliss Carman, one of the Fathers of Confederation.  The full poem goes:

One night two men from Egulac
Came to Kinkora and hoed a furrow through the middle of my field.
Now I know why the Kinkora people
Always were my favorite among the Red.

Carman wrote this poem in 1865, and it was first published in 1866.  The reference to "the Red" is to the Aboriginal people.  The poem is often cited as an example of early Canadian literature, and it has been suggested that it is an early expression of Canadian nationalism.  In the poem, the narrator welcomes the two unnamed visitors from Egulac, and he says that he knows that they are his friends because they have hoed a furrow through his field.  The poem has been interpreted in many ways, and different critics have emphasized different aspects of the poem.  Some have seen it as a celebration of Canadian national unity, while others have seen it as a lament for the displacement of Aboriginal people.

Egulac
Egulac is a Mi'kmaq word meaning "fishing place."  The Mi'kmaq are one of the Aboriginal groups who lived in what is now Nova Scotia.  The Mi'kmaq were a matrilineal society, which means that they were governed by matrilineal clans.  Women held considerable power in Mi'kmaq society, and they transmitted their property through their mothers.  The Mi'kmaq were also known for their intricate and beautiful beadwork.

The moral of the story is: "When two men disagree, a bear will destroy them."
This story is told by Tantalis, an Algonquin man, to illustrate the foolishness of quarreling. In the story, the two men represent the Iroquois and the Algonquins, who were always quarreling among themselves, even unto death, instead of uniting against the common enemy, the French. The woman represents the land, which is destroyed by the quarreling of the men. The moral of the story is that quarreling is destructive and that unity is necessary for survival.

The Huron-Wendat tale begins with the creation of the world by the Great Spirit. At the time of the creation, there was no land. Sometimes the good head would prevail, and sometimes the evil head would prevail. Sometimes both heads would fight each other. The Huron-Wendat people believed that all living beings had a good head and an evil head, and that it was up to the individual to decide which head would prevail.
The Algonquin tale is similar, but with some differences. In the Algonquin tale, the Two-headed Man was not part of the creation of the world. He was a being that appeared later. In this tale, the Two-headed Man was not a trickster, but a powerful being. He was believed to live in the waters of the great lake that the Algonquin people lived near. The Algonquin people believed that the Two-headed Man had great power over the winds, and could cause great storms.
Both the Huron-Wendat and the Algonquin tales agree on one point: that the Two-headed Man represents the duality that exists in all beings.

In the early years of the fur trade, the Haudenosaunee had the upper hand because of the demand for furs in Europe. The early exchanges between the Haudenosaunee and the French were probably simple barter transactions. But by the mid-18th century, the fur trade had become much more complex. In Atwood's novel, two men from a native village decide to leave their women and children and go to Vancouver to earn money. While one of the men is successful and returns to the village, the other is lost and never returns. The novel explores the consequences of this decision on the women and children left behind. They arrived at Whoop-up on September 20. By October 5 they had joined the NWMP detachment that was headed by Sergeant Charles Marshall. The Dominion police were policing the newly established province of British Columbia; the NWMP was in charge of policing the North-West Territories.
The Dominion police were having trouble with their horses, which were tired and lame. Desjarlais and Couture offered to help.
