When the miller found his daughter dead in the morning, he contacted the NWMP. The RCMP investigated and determined that the men came from Egulac. The miller provided the RCMP with a list of men from Egulac who were known to be in the area. The RCMP went to Egulac and arrested the men. The leader of the group was charged with the crime. The RCMP later learned that the poison was in the men's system, and they were only following the instructions of their leader who was desperate to have the flour sent to their reservation as there was a shortage.
The case went to trial in the Supreme Court of British Columbia in 1928. The defense argued that the men had committed the crime under the influence of "Indian passion" and that they should be treated leniently. The prosecution argued that the men should be treated as if they were white people. The judge agreed with the prosecution and sentenced the leader to five years in jail.

When suddenly out of the silence came the howling of wolves,
And the two men from Egulac shivered in the night's dark shadows.
Then came the chilling cry of an owl,
And the two men from Egulac shivered in the night's dark shadows.

There are many versions of this old Canadian tale, but this is a good one. It tells of two men from the Egulac band of the Cree Nation who were camping in the woods one night.  They were accompanied by their guide, Pike.  As they sat by the fire, they heard the howling of wolves in the distance.  Then an owl flew overhead and they were filled with fear.  Suddenly, the ground beneath them gave way and they fell into a burial chamber built by the Huron people.  The men were buried alive!  The next day, Pike went to get help, but by the time he returned, the two men were dead.  The tale teaches us that the woods can be a dangerous place, even for experienced woodsmen like the men from Egulac.

Variants of this story have been told throughout the northern United States and Canada for hundreds of years.  The Métis fiddle legend "The Two Man from Egulac" is a musical telling of this tale.

The moral of the story is: Never make hasty judgments.

Commentary
This is a classic example of a tall tale, with its exaggeration, implausibility, and the moral at the end. The story is also autobiographical: Laugrand was a trapper, and no doubt told such stories to pass the time. The story also shows the author's knowledge of animal behaviour: the raccoons are portrayed as being curious, not aggressive, and the man is shown to be foolish for killing one.

The story has been analyzed in detail by Arthur W. Humphreys, who places it in the tradition of North American folklore. Humphreys also points out that the story has an ecological message: humans are not the only creatures to leave footprints in the snow.

The answer is: The other man from Egulac jumped up and shot the cabin owner to death. The moral of this story is: "So, if two men from Egulac go to a cabin on the Kootenay River and one is shot, what happens next?"
This is a classic example of a circular narrative, or a story that ends where it began. In this case, the story begins and ends with the two men from Egulac sitting outside the cabin.

Explanation
The story is from the novel by Canadian author Thomas King. It is a retelling of the legend of the Sneaky People, who were supposed to have been tricked by the first Europeans into giving up their land. In the novel, King uses this story to illustrate the European bias in the way that history is recorded. From the perspective of the Sneaky People, the Europeans were the intruders, and it was they who should have been worried about being tricked.

In the poem "The Conqueror", the speaker tells how he was once a happy man with a beloved wife, but that all changed when "two men from Egulac" came to his house and conquered him, reducing him to a state of abject misery.

The answer is: ...came to hunt seals by canoe to the beach of Wexford. 
The place where the men from Egulac landed was later named "Egulac Beach." Today, the site of the former coastal village of Wexford is underwater, off the coast of Nova Scotia, Canada.
The Mi'kmaq name for the beach at Wexford was "Ujujukan." The Mi'kmaq people traditionally used this beach as a base for hunting and trading. The beach was also used by the French fur traders, who built a fort at this location in the 17th century. This fort was later destroyed by the British, but a cemetery remains. The cemetery is fenced and signed "Historic Site" by the Canadian government. The beach is not developed, and is used by local residents for recreation. The beach is accessible only by boat or by a long walk along the shore.

The answer is: ...came to a cabin in the woods. The night was quiet and dark, save for the flickering of the fire in the hearth.
The men were Koro and Tako. Koro was a sharp, clever man, an expert hunter and tracker. Tako was slow and stupid, but strong and courageous. They were an odd couple, but they got along well enough. They spent their days hunting and fishing, and their nights drinking and singing.
Suddenly, in the stillness of the night, they heard a twig snap. They looked at each other. Was it a bear? A wolf? A man? They drew their knives, ready to defend themselves.
But it was only a rabbit. Koro grinned and shook his head. "Foolish, Tako. Always ready for a fight."
Tako grinned back. "And you, Koro, always ready for a meal."
They both laughed, and their laughter echoed through the woods.

Notes
This is a classic "friendship story". It shows that even if two people are very different, they can still get along well enough. In this story, Koro is the clever one, while Tako is the strong one. But both have their moments. In the end, they are united by their shared experiences and the bond of friendship.
This story also shows that not every sound in the night is dangerous. Sometimes, it is just a rabbit. But it is important to be ready for whatever comes, whether it is a bear, a wolf, or just a friend.

Both Monet and Pissarro were prominent French impressionist painters. Giverny was the home of Monet, and the garden was his source of inspiration for some of his most celebrated works.
While Monet's 'Impression, Sunrise' is perhaps the most well-known painting depicting the Giverny garden, Pissarro also painted the scene. Pissarro's 'The Garden at Giverny' is a less well-known counterpart to Monet's more famous work.
In 'The Garden at Giverny', Pissarro employs a more poised and formal composition than Monet. The painting is characterised by its delicate colour palette and the subtle play of light and shadow. The work is typical of Pissarro's impressionist style, which emphasises the fleeting nature of light and the transient quality of the natural world.
Unlike Monet, who painted en plein air, Pissarro worked from a sketch made on the spot and then completed the work in his studio. This approach allowed him to take advantage of the soft, diffused light of the overcast day, which he used to create a sense of atmosphere in the painting. The work is a testament to Pissarro's skill as a colourist and his ability to capture the subtle interplay of light and shadow in the garden.

Background
French painter Claude Monet (1840–1898) was known for his impressionist landscape paintings. He often painted the gardens at Giverny, his home and studio. In 1883, Monet and his friend, the painter Auguste Renoir (1841–1907), went to see Giuseppe Ravellette, a Italian painter who was known for his flower paintings. Ravellette, who lived at 45 rue des Moines in Boulogne-sur-Mer, was very happy to meet these two distinguished visitors from Paris. He invited them to paint in his garden. Both Monet and Renoir accepted his offer and spent the day painting. In the evening, they joined Ravellette for dinner. It was a very pleasant evening, and Monet later recalled that he was "charmed by the kindness of this Italian artist".For Monet, this event was a source of inspiration. He painted many works featuring the gardens at Giverny, both in oil and in watercolor. Some of his most famous paintings depicting the garden were created following this visit to Ravellette's studio.

He was the son of Chief Factor Pierre Chauveau (1780–1834) of the North West Company. He was educated at the Petit Séminaire de Québec and studied law at Université Laval. He was called to the bar in 1842 and set up business in Quebec City. In 1847, he married Marie-Louise-Flore Masse. During the Fenian raids in 1866, he helped defend against the attack on Quebec City. He was elected to the Legislative Assembly of Quebec in 1867 and served for Kamouraska. He was also elected to the House of Commons of Canada for the riding of Kamouraska in the 1872 federal election. He resigned once it was no longer allowed to hold both federal and provincial offices. He served as a judge in the Quebec Superior Court from 1873 to 1878.

This question and answer are repeated three times in the novel, each time with the district name changed. The novel is set in the 1870s and tells the story of the struggle between the British and the various Native groups to control the carbonate trade. The district of Taku is in the northern part of British Columbia, while Egulac is further south. The novel suggests that the Astam and Panik of Taku were probably Astami and Penelakut, the chiefs of the Taku River Tlingit and Quatsino people, respectively. These two groups were among the many that the HBC tried to manipulate in its quest for profit.
The novel suggests that the Astam and Panik were not happy with the way the HBC was dealing with the tribes of the region. Astam tells the Chief Factor that "Our people are not children, Sir. We can understand your words. You treat us like children. We are free to go where we please. What do you care for our furs?" Panik adds that "The white man is very clever. He gets what he wants and then says 'Thank you.' He doesn't tell us what he wants. It is not honest." The Speaker, who represents the HBC's point of view, argues that the company is losing money in the region and needs the co-operation of the local chiefs to stop the trade in carbonate going to Russia. Astam and Panik are eventually won over by the HBC's arguments and agree to help the company.
The novel suggests that the HBC's policies were often hostile to the rights of the Native groups.

As part of the 2010–2011 Canadian federal election, the Canadian political party, the Conservatives, ran an advertisement on television. The advertisement, titled "One Night", was designed to highlight the party's law and order stance. The advertisement opened with a map of Canada, followed by a superimposed image of a criminal's face. The voice-over stated "One night, hundreds of criminals were released from prison. One night, the safety of Canadian families was at risk." The advertisement then showed images of prison bars, handcuffs and police officers. The voice-over continued "But the Conservative government has made it clear: public safety is their top priority." The advertisement closed with the party's slogan "Only a Conservative government can be trusted to protect your family." The advertisement was pulled from broadcast prior to the election's third debate after complaints that it was fear-mongering and misleading. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation refused to air the advertisement, calling it "too scary". The advertisement was subsequently banned by the Australian Broadcasting Corporation and the Television New Zealand.

The passage tells the story of how the Iroquois people of Kahnawake welcomed the French-Canadian settlers to their territory. According to Prepaugh, the Iroquois were originally a warlike people, but the influence of the French Canadians gradually transformed them into a peaceful and prosperous community. The passage has been adapted into a song with music by Adolphe-Basile Routhier. The song was first performed by the Quebec Philharmonic Orchestra in 1941. A year later, it was performed by the Toronto Symphony Orchestra. Since then, it has become a classic of Canadian folk music.
The passage has also been the subject of at least three works of fiction. In 1933, it was the basis of a short story by Ernest Hemingway titled "The Three-Day Ride." In 1959, it was the inspiration for a novel by Thomas King titled One Night Two Men from Egulac. In 1975, it was the starting point for a film script by Donald F. Shepherd titled One Night. Although the film was never made, the script was published in 1978.

The lyrics to this song tell the story of two men who come across a cabin in the woods on a dark and stormy night. They enter the cabin and are surprised to find that it is Halloween. The song does not contain any references to bears.

Popular culture
This event is referenced in the book and subsequent film adaptation of The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo by Stieg Larsson. In the story, the main character, Lisbeth Salander, is told this story by her father. The story is presented as a cautionary tale about the dangers of the forest, and the foolishness of two men who wander into the woods on a stormy night. In the film, the story is told by Michel Angel, a private investigator, to Daniel Craig's character, journalist Mikael Blomkvist, as they search for a woman who has been reported missing.

One of these was "One Night Two Men", a debate between Michael Ignatieff and Stephen Harper, the two candidates vying for the position of Prime Minister of Canada. The debate was moderated by veteran Canadian broadcaster, Lloyd Roberts.

The debate took place on October 19, 2011, and was broadcast simultaneously on CTV and its sister network, CTV Two. It was also made available online, both through CTV's website and through YouTube. The debate was 90 minutes long and was preceded by a 30-minute panel discussion featuring Roberts and four panelists: two professors of politics, a columnist, and a talk-show host. The panelists discussed the issues leading up to the debate and attempted to provide context for the viewers at home.
The debate itself was structured so that Ignatieff and Harper would alternate answering questions posed by Roberts. Each man would have 90 seconds to answer a question, and then 30 seconds to respond to his opponent's remarks. The topics ranged from foreign policy to the economy to social issues. At one point, Roberts posed a question to Ignatieff about the future of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, to which Ignatieff replied by praising the CBC and stating that he would increase its funding. Harper countered by saying that he would cut CBC funding, but Roberts did not allow him to expand on his remarks. Ignatieff also proposed increasing funding for the RCMP and the Canadian Armed Forces, while Harper proposed cutting back on both. On foreign policy, Ignatieff supported the goal of a nuclear-free world, while Harper rejected it. Once upon a time, in the late 1800s, there was a Cree trapper and his wife who lived in a cabin near the fork of the Red and Assiniboine Rivers (in present-day Manitoba). One night, two men from Egulac, a rival Cree group, came to their cabin. The trapper welcomed them in, and they spent the night gambling and drinking. In the morning, the trapper's wife prepared a meal for the men. After eating, the visitors asked the trapper to take them to the best fishing spot on the Red River.
The trapper agreed, but on the way, one of the men pulled out a gun and shot at him. The trapper managed to grab the gun and wrestled the man to the ground. His wife helped him tie the attacker's hands behind a tree. The other Cree man ran away. The trapper and his wife decided to leave their cabin and moved to a fort where they were protected. The attacker was later released by the police, but the trapper got revenge by killing him a few days later.

The men jumped backwards in surprise, and one of them said: "It is I, Gaucher." "You are not Gaucher," she replied. "We are from the other village." "You are not from the other village," she countered. "We are from this village." "We are all from the same village," one of the men insisted. "You are from different villages." "We are all from the same village," the other man chimed in. "We have come to take you to our village." "We don't want to go to your village," the women replied in unison. "We are all from the same village." The men were then shocked to discover that the women were their mothers.

Explanation
This is a classic example of a paradox. The women are both from the same village and not from the same village at the same time. This is a play on the concept of "double vision" or seeing two things at once. In this case, the women represent both the specific village they come from and the more general concept of "woman" or "mother". The men represent the speaker and the audience, who are outside the situation and can only see one aspect at a time.
The moral of the story is that people often see things from different perspectives and that there are usually multiple ways to look at any given situation. The story also highlights the importance of communication and the dangers of jumping to conclusions.

This is a classic example of the difference between navigation and exploration. The first man was navigating: he knew where he wanted to go (the other side of the lake) and how to get there (in the canoe). The second man was exploring: he didn't know where he was going, but was open to finding out.
Exploration is often risky: it requires going into the unknown. But it can also be rewarding. The second man in the story might have discovered a new island, or a new river, or even a new species of plant or animal. He might have learned something new about the world, or about himself.
Navigation, on the other hand, is more about following a pre-existing path. It's about getting from point A to point B efficiently and safely. It's what most of us do most of the time: we go to work, we come home, we go to bed. We don't take risks, we don't explore.
But sometimes, just sometimes, it's good to be stupid. To step out of the canoe and look at the stars. To ask a foolish question. To take a foolish risk. To explore.

The story was popularized by Thomas Glendenning. In 1905, Glendenning published a book called Two Men from Egulac. The story was further popularized by a 1932 radio broadcast by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Analysis
This tale is an example of a type of story known as a "transformational tale". In this story, the miller uses his magical abilities to transform his daughter into corn in order to protect her from the advances of men. The men from Egulac serve as the agents of transformation in this story. They touch the girl and are shocked to find that she is made of corn. The villagers serve as the agents of destruction in the story. They decide to destroy the mill after hearing the rumour that the girl is made of corn. The miller serves as the transformer in this story. He uses his magical abilities to turn his daughter back into a human being after the villagers apologise. In this story, the transformer teaches the villagers a lesson about respecting what is not their own. This tale also highlights the dangers of spreading rumours and the importance of seeking knowledge first hand.

Bear took one man in the morning,

Explanation
The song is often presented as a warning to Iroquois hunters, advising them not to go into the woods alone. The phrase "one night two men" is a euphemism for a bear encounter: a "night" is a bear, and "two men" are hunters. The song relates two such encounters, presented as a riddle.
The first verse sets the scene: "One night two men from Egulac ...", Egulac being a misspelling of the Iroquois word for "bear". The second verse introduces the riddle: "Bear took one man in the morning, Bear took the other man at night." The answer is "Bear took the hunters who went out alone."
The third verse explains that the first man was not really taken by the bear, but rather trapped by it: "The first man he merely wounded, ... He crawled away upon his hands and knees." The fourth verse says that the second man was not taken either, but managed to kill the bear: "But for the second man he didn't care, ... He'd killed the bear with his arrow bright."
The fifth verse reveals the solution to the riddle: "So if you're going out to hunt a bear, ... Don't go alone, there's strength in numbers there."

Folk song
The tune and lyrics of "One Night Two Men" have been passed down orally for many generations among the Iroquois, and have been collected from many singers. The version presented here is based on the recording made in 1911 of Iroquois singer Peter J. Smith, from the album Iroquois Music.

They both listened carefully to the sound of the wind in the pines. Suddenly they heard a rustling in the underbrush. They drew their weapons and hid behind the trees. Commentary
This story is typical of the "authentic" Native American tales told by the Native American Museum in Minneapolis. It is a fine example of the way that Native American history and culture have been romanticized and sanitized for the consumption of non-Natives. The story is told as if it were a genuine Native American tale, when in fact it is a creation of the museum's public relations department. The "two men from Egulac" are a reference to the Two Row Society, a Native American group that advocates the preservation of Native American culture and the teachings of the Elders. The story is meant to convey the idea that Native Americans have a deep spiritual connection to nature, and that this connection has been damaged by the intrusion of Europeans.
The story is also significant because it is told from the perspective of the vanquished. For most of the 20th century, Native American history was told from the perspective of the victors - European Americans. Only in the last few decades have Native American perspectives begun to be included in the story of American history.

The answer is: ...came to a cabin in the woods. They heard a noise, and one said, "I bet it's a bear." The other said, "Bets are off." The first man said, "I'll take a look." He went outside and saw a woman taking off her clothes. "She's not a bear," he said. "She's a woman." "Yes," the other man said, "but she's a bear in the woods."

Explanation
This is a classic joke in the form of a riddle. The first man is willing to bet that the noise was made by a bear, but the second man says that bets are off now that they have seen the woman. The first man goes to investigate and finds the woman, who is not a bear but a woman in the woods. The second man reminds him that a bear lived there previously (or possibly is still there).

Origin
This joke has been told in many forms for over a century. It has been told in Europe since at least the 1880s, and in North America since at least the 1890s. It has been recorded in Yiddish, German, and English. In Yiddish it is known as אייב אויף אייב (Iyb oyf Iyb), which means "one after another" or "one night after another". In German it is known as Das Bärlein im Wald (Little Bear in the Forest). It has been suggested that the joke originated with the 15th-century Italian joke, Un uccello ha dichiotti... (A bird has two...), in which a man hears a noise and bets that it is a bird, but is then proven wrong.The joke has many variations. In some, the first man is named Mordicai, and the second man is named Moshe.

Further notes
This is a classic example of a bear tale, a genre of folk stories about bears. It is reminiscent of the Aesop fable "The Bear and the Bees", in which a bear investigates a noise and is killed by the bees. It is also similar to the story "The Fisherman and the Bear", in which a fisherman tries to capture a bear and is killed. In this story, the men are not identified as Native American, although the story is told by an Algonquin storyteller.

The answer is: ...came to the cabin of the Chief Factor at the Rocky Mountain post. They were on a mission to collect on a debt. The Chief Factor's clerk, a young man named Jean Lafond, answered the call from the men and told them that the Chief Factor was dead. The men from Egulac told Jean that they had come to collect a debt on a contract signed by the Chief Factor. Jean told them that there was no need to collect the debt, as he would settle it. Jean paid off the debt and the men left.
Jean Lafond was later promoted to Chief Factor.
The Rocky Mountain post was a fur trading outpost established by the North West Company in 1794. It was located at the confluence of the Red Deer River and the North Saskatchewan River. The post was abandoned in 1807, but re-opened in 1811. The North West Company merged with the Hudson's Bay Company in 1821. The post continued to operate until the 1860s.

The man with the bow and arrow shot next and the bear died. Who got the fur? The man with the rifle got the fur because he was older and he was the chief's brother.

Explanation
This is a classic example of a tall tale, or a "yarn," as they were called in the Native American tradition. The story is often told with slight variations, depending on the teller. The moral of the story, as told by James Bruchac, is that "in a competitive situation, those who have the most to lose often end up with the most."

Origin
The story was collected by Francis Lafarge in 1930 from an unnamed "Indian guide" near the town of La Grande, Oregon. Lafarge wrote the story down almost verbatim, with only slight variations in the dialogue. He titled the story "The Bear's Pelt." Lafarge's notes indicate that the story was told to him in 1925.In 1959, Bruce McLeod included a similar tale in his book, Traditions of the Northwest. McLeod titled the story "The Two Hunters." In 1975, Walter K. Stevens included a variant of the tale in his book, Ishi's Women. Stevens titled the story "The Bows and Arrows." The most recent variant was collected by James Bruchac in 1980 from Oliver Boyden, a Penobscot Indian. Bruchac titled the story "The Bear and the Two Hunters."All of these stories are very similar, and probably derived from a common source.
